chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
title: Walter Bales, the union and the two-piano rich man
summary: A white millionaire and pianist, Walter Bales, read the write-up and sought McShann out through the union; he had played two pianos with Basie.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: That was our first write-up, the first write-up, and from that write-up, there was a fellow that was a good friend of Basie's named Walter Bales.

And he saw this write-up and so he called down to the union. See, but I wasn't in the union then. Called down to the union and told them, says, "Listen, send that musician, have him to get in touch with me and come out to my place out here and get in touch with me." And so the union sent a guy by the name of Ross L. Claxton out there. So when Ross came out to Mr. Bales' place, Mr. Bales says, "Are you Jay McShann?" He says, "No, I'm Ross L. Claxton." He says, "Well, no, I didn't send for you. I told them to send McShann out here. Why didn't they send McShann?" So Claxton says, "Well, he's not in the union and so the union sent me out."

So Walter Bales said, 'Well, here,' he gave him some money for his troubles and 'here's your cab fare,' and you know. So Walter Bales called back down to the union next day and says, 'Listen, why is it you guys sent somebody else? I asked you to send McShann out,' you know. So then they made an excuse. They said, 'Oh, we'll get in touch with him and we'll have him to come out. But he wasn't a member of the union, and that's the reason we did that.' So, okay, so finally they contacted me and told me to go out and see Mr. Bales.
Well, Mr. Bales and Basie used to get together with the two pianos, you know.
Oh, Bales was a piano player too, was he?
Yes, see, and he helped Basie a lot, you know.
What did he do? What is he?
Well, he was a -- oh, a guy that had a lot of money, rich and had real estate --

No, white fella. He owned about a third of Kansas City and then he was also -- owned a big portion of the Travelers Insurance, Hartford, Connecticut, you know? He was big -- and so, but he liked piano and so that's how he and Basie would get together and they'd go down to Jenkins and play two pianos, you know, and do duets together

and come out and he had a recording thing that he'd play something, record it, play it back, you know, like that. So, he had me to come out and he was telling me about how he and Basie used to do and so we would, you know, do the same thing, you know, and so he told me one night, says, "Look, they're having a thing over at the country club. You'd like to come over there and a certain part down there in the basement, they just have piano alone. So they got a couple of other bands up on the other floors. But if you want to make that," I said, "Yeah, I'll be glad to make it."
